editorNote: A week of retrenchment at Apple and literary ambition on the home computer.
morningLine: Apple counts the cost; poets find a place on disk.

lead.headline: Apple cuts one-fifth of workforce as first quarterly loss looms
lead.dek: Three plants face closure as the personal-computer maker lowers its break-even point.
body: Apple Computer is cutting 1,200 jobs and closing three of its six production plants, according to the June 24 Computerworld. The recently announced restructuring removes roughly one-fifth of the workforce as the company prepares for what it expects will be its first quarterly loss in eight years.

The closures cover Carrollton, Texas; Garden Grove, California; and Millstreet, Ireland, over the coming three months. Manufacturing accounts for 60 percent of the layoffs. Research and development is spared, although sales, marketing, finance and administration also face reductions.

President John Sculley says the measures should significantly reduce the company’s break-even point. Restructuring charges are expected to push the quarter ending June 30 into the red; an analyst estimate of a $15 million after-tax loss remains a forecast, not a published final result.

The cuts follow a reorganization combining Apple II and Macintosh production divisions and removing chairman Steven P. Jobs from operational control. Jobs has not resigned from Apple. With approximately 4,600 employees expected to remain, the company is seeking a leaner manufacturing and marketing structure without abandoning research.

stories.headline: Electronic novels recruit poets as well as science-fiction stars
body: A poet and a science-fiction humorist are helping turn the adventure game into an electronic novel. June’s COMPUTE!'s Gazette profiles Robert Pinsky’s work with Synapse on Mindwheel alongside Douglas Adams and Steve Meretzky’s collaboration on The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. These are accounts of development and design, not announcements of releases this week.

Synapse sought writers who did not already know adventure-game conventions. Pinsky, head of Berkeley’s creative-writing program and poetry editor of The New Republic, worked with programmers credited in the magazine as William Mataga and Steve Hales. Mindwheel comes in a hardback book with a disk, and the printed material supplies information needed during play.

The attraction is language rather than another screen full of pictures. Synapse calls its system BTZ, Better Than ZORK, and pursues more vocabulary and richer parsing. That is a design ambition and a tradeoff against memory-hungry graphics, not proof that every text adventure outclasses every illustrated game.

Adams describes planning in Boston, electronic-mail exchanges from England, a London work session and more testing in Boston. The months-long partnership makes the modem as much a writer’s tool as a hobbyist’s accessory.

stories.headline: Commodore 128 promises three computing worlds in one box
body: The Commodore 128 promises continuity as well as expansion. Tom R. Halfhill’s June COMPUTE! hands-on report describes a machine that can run existing C64 software, enter a native 128K environment with BASIC 7.0, or use a Z80-based CP/M mode aimed at business applications.

Native and CP/M modes offer 80-column text. RGB output and the faster 1571 disk drive give the buyer more to consider than memory alone, while compatibility with C64 peripherals protects part of an existing investment.

The report follows a mid-March visit and expected June store availability with intended retail below $300. Those are advance expectations, not a verified June 24 launch or a confirmed dealer transaction. Buyers should distinguish the promise of three computing worlds from the software and equipment actually on a dealer’s shelf.

stories.headline: Commodore LCD portable slips beyond September
body: Commodore’s LCD portable is running later than expected. The June Gazette reports that the prototype shown at January’s Consumer Electronics Show is now expected sometime after September, rather than midsummer. Marketing vice president Frank Leonardi denies that the project has been shelved.

The proposed five-and-a-half-pound machine combines an 80-by-16-character display, 32K RAM and 96K ROM with eight built-in applications: word processor, file manager, spreadsheet, address book, scheduler, calculator, memo pad and terminal emulator.

A built-in 300-baud modem and support for Commodore serial peripherals, including 1541 and 1571 drives, make it more than a pocket notebook. The reported $600 price and timetable remain plans for a prototype, not evidence of a shipping product.

curiosity.summary: Synapse sells an electronic novel whose physical book is part of play.

undergroundDesk.headline: Computer-trespass sentence tests new federal law
undergroundDesk.dek: Probation, a fine and equipment forfeiture follow unauthorized Forest Service access.
body: Computerworld’s June 24 report describes the June 14 sentencing of Philip Gonzalez Fadriquela, 26, of Los Angeles, after a May guilty plea to unauthorized access to Forest Service computers in Colorado. The sentence includes three years probation, a $3,000 fine, 200 hours of community service, equipment forfeiture and an explanatory statement to the agency.

Prosecutor Cathy Goodwin presents the case as evidence that convictions can be obtained under the 1984 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Defense lawyer Robert Booms challenges the law’s breadth and says his client did not use stored information. The report mentions hacker bulletin boards but names no board, crew or handle.
